newsitem.title: ITALY: Separatist Bossi begins his march to split Italy.
newsitem.headline: Separatist Bossi begins his march to split Italy.

text.p: Separatist leader Umberto Bossi launched a weekend of demonstrations along Italy's River Po on Friday that will lead to a planned proclamation of "independence" on Sunday for his self-styled northern republic.

The Northern League party leader filled a Venetian glass flask with water at this mountain source of Italy's longest river to begin a three-day "March to the Sea" which he hopes will draw at least one million followers of his breakaway plan.

The weekend of demonstrations, expected to be met by counter-rallies by supporters of Italian unity, is due to end on Sunday with Bossi's proclamation in Venice of a "federal republic of Padania", the name he gives his self-styled state.

"Water is the source of all things, of life, of Padania," said Bossi, dressed casually with a pink ribbon pinned to his woollen cardigan in an echo of the ribbons Italians place on their front doors to celebrate the birth of a child.
"This is a symbolic act. This water from the Po, from Padania, will be on the stage when the independence of Padania is declared on Sunday," he said to shouts of "Bossi, Bossi" and "Freedom".
The flask of water, part of Bossi's attempt to create a symbolism for an idea that has no ethnic or linguistic basis, was placed in a green box to be carried by Bossi along the Po.

About 200 people, most of them from the media, gathered at the 2,040 metre (6,690 ft) high mountain plateau near the border with France to watch the ceremony. Bossi was escorted by police and stewards from his own green-shirted security detachment.

Bossi has brushed off evidence that his separatist push has little support, even among the League's own voters. One opinion poll published on Friday showed only 7.6 percent of Italians were in favour of splitting the nation.

The firebrand separatist has said he hopes Sunday's symbolic proclamation will be followed within a year by full independence for a region encompassing the richest areas of Italy and its industrial heartland.

His campaign has been condemned across the political spectrum. All Bossi's opponents say federal reform is the best response to popular frustration with high taxes, government bureaucracy and public sector inefficiency.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who heads a centre-left government installed in May, said earlier on Friday that Bossi's project had "no roots in the past and no future".
Condemnation also came from former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, whose stormy seven-month government coalition with Bossi's League in 1994 ended in a bitter political divorce.

Berlusconi, leader of the main centre-right opposition alliance, expressed understanding for the northern discontent that has drawn the League support but said secession was a non-starter and accused Bossi of sowing "ethnic hatred".
"It has happened in other countries. We must prevent it from happening in Italy," Berlusconi said in an apparent reference to the bloodshed that tore apart Italy's neighbour Yugoslavia.
Bossi's most prominent internal dissident, Irene Pivetti, who was summarily expelled from the League on Thursday, said Bossi was making a political fool of himself.
"Nothing will have changed for Italy on Monday. The brouhaha will be over but the problems will remain," she said.
